questions.q: What design question does this lesson say matters most for automated containment, beyond whatever a SOAR platform can technically automate?
options: Which vendor's SOAR platform is cheapest to license
How many playbooks a security team can write per quarter
Whether automation should be disabled entirely during business hours
When automated isolation should fire first versus when it should wait for a human to approve it
questions.explain: The SOAR platform can automate either path; the design decision is which specific actions should fire automatically and which should wait for human approval, based on blast radius.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an automated containment action has its own blast radius?
options: Because a false positive on a low-impact action and a false positive on a high-impact action, like isolating a shared production resource, cause very different amounts of damage
Because automated actions never have any real-world effect
Because blast radius only applies to attackers, never to defensive responses
Because SOAR platforms cannot be configured to isolate production systems
questions.explain: Applying the blast-radius concept to the response itself: a false positive isolating one workstation is cheap, while a false positive isolating a shared production resource creates an outage of its own.

questions.q: According to this lesson's tiered-response pattern, which action is a reasonable candidate for auto-containment with no human approval?
options: Revoking a certificate trusted by multiple applications
Disabling a shared service account that many pipelines depend on
Isolating a single end-user workstation flagged by EDR with high-confidence malware indicators
Cutting off a network segment that other production systems depend on
questions.explain: Isolating one workstation with a high-confidence detection has low blast radius — the worst case of a false positive is recoverable in minutes and affects one person.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that detection confidence alone is the wrong axis for deciding whether an action should be automated?
options: Because detection confidence is impossible to measure in practice
Because a high-confidence detection on a high-blast-radius resource still deserves a human in the loop — the cost of being wrong should drive the decision, not just the odds of being right
Because confidence scores are only available for malware detections, not credential-based ones
Because human analysts are always slower than automation regardless of confidence
questions.explain: The dividing line should be blast radius, not confidence, because even a confident detection on a high-impact resource can be wrong, and the cost of being wrong there is what matters most.

questions.q: How does this lesson say automated isolation closes the loop on the rest of the chapter?
options: It is built directly on the blast-radius estimates from Lesson 14 and the lateral-movement controls from Lesson 15, acting as the fast last line that contains what got through without becoming its own blast-radius problem
It replaces the need for blast-radius estimates and lateral-movement controls entirely
It only applies to lessons outside this chapter, such as identity verification
It eliminates the need for a human decision point in any containment scenario
questions.explain: Automated isolation is scoped using the same blast-radius thinking from Lesson 14 and responds to the lateral-movement techniques from Lesson 15, serving as a fast last resort rather than a replacement for either.
